body:
Industry as a major energy consumer

Gujarat's manufacturing economy requires electricity and fuels for different purposes. Electrical energy operates motors, pumps, compressors, lighting, refrigeration and manufacturing machinery. Fuels such as natural gas or coal supply heat for industrial processes. Petroleum and natural gas can also provide chemical feedstocks that become part of manufactured products.

An industry's total energy requirement is therefore broader than its electricity bill. A factory may reduce electricity purchases without reducing its use of gas, or it may replace a fuel-fired process with an electrical one and increase its electricity demand.

Three different ways an industry uses energy resources

  • Electricity: Runs equipment such as motors, pumps and production machinery.
  • Fuel for process heat: Supplies the heat needed in operations such as firing, drying, heating or steam production.
  • Chemical feedstock: Provides raw material that is chemically transformed into products, such as natural gas used in ammonia manufacture.

The distinction between fuel and feedstock is particularly important. When natural gas is burnt in a furnace, it is being used as a fuel. When it provides the hydrogen-containing raw material for ammonia production, it is being used as a feedstock. The same resource can serve both purposes.

Examples from Gujarat's industrial geography

Industrial areaImportant activitiesEnergy connection
JamnagarPetroleum refining and petrochemicalsCrude-oil processing, industrial fuels and feedstocks
Dahej and BharuchChemicals, petrochemicals and related industriesElectricity, natural gas and chemical feedstocks
MorbiCeramic manufacturingNatural gas and other fuels for process heat; electricity for machinery
SuratTextiles and other manufacturingElectricity for machinery and energy for industrial processes

Morbi's ceramic industry provides a clear example of industrial dependence on reliable fuel supply. Ceramic production requires substantial heat for firing products in kilns. A disruption or sharp change in the availability or price of gas can therefore affect industrial production.

In a statement dated 23 April 2026, the company then known as Gujarat Gas Limited described efforts to maintain natural-gas supply to Morbi's ceramic industries during supply-related difficulties. The episode illustrates the connection between international gas markets, distribution networks and local industrial activity. It does not mean that every ceramic unit uses only natural gas.

Industrial demand and electricity demand

Industrial activity is a major source of electricity demand in Gujarat. The NITI Aayog-linked India Climate and Energy Dashboard identifies industry as the largest electricity-consumption category in Gujarat's 2023–24 consumption data. The same dashboard identifies domestic consumers as the largest category by consumer count in its 2024–25 distribution profile.

These statements are not contradictory. The first concerns how much electricity is consumed; the second concerns how many customers are connected. A comparatively small number of large factories may use more electricity than a much larger number of individual households.

Why reliable energy matters for industrial production

Some industrial processes operate continuously or depend on a stable temperature. Unexpected interruptions may stop machinery, interrupt production or damage work in progress. Reliable electricity and fuel supplies therefore support industrial productivity.

Industrial energy security involves several separate conditions: sufficient energy must be available, it must reach the factory through suitable infrastructure, and its cost must be manageable. A power station or LNG terminal located elsewhere in Gujarat does not automatically guarantee that every industrial consumer can obtain uninterrupted supply.

Prelims focus

  • Jamnagar is an important petroleum-refining and petrochemical centre.
  • Dahej and Bharuch are associated with chemical and related manufacturing industries.
  • Morbi is an important ceramic manufacturing centre.
  • Natural gas can be used both as an industrial fuel and as a chemical feedstock.
  • Industry was the largest electricity-consumption category in Gujarat's 2023–24 data reported by the India Climate and Energy Dashboard.
  • Trap: The sector with the most electricity consumers need not be the sector that consumes the most electricity.

[References: NCERT, Class 12 Geography, India: People and Economy, Chapter 8, 'Manufacturing Industries,' section on industrial location and manufacturing activities; NCERT, Class 11 Economics, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 8, 'Infrastructure,' printed pp. 140–149; India Climate and Energy Dashboard, NITI Aayog, 'Gujarat State Profile,' electricity distribution indicators for FY 2023–24 and FY 2024–25, consulted 16 November 2026; Gujarat Gas Limited, press release on Morbi ceramic industry and gas supply dated 23 April 2026.]

title: Industrial Energy Demand in Gujarat

body:
From generating station to final consumer

Electricity is generated at power stations but must be transported to the places where it is required. A typical supply system contains generation, transmission and distribution.

  1. Generation: A power station converts an energy source into electricity.
  2. Transmission: High-voltage networks carry bulk electricity over substantial distances and connect major parts of the power system.
  3. Distribution: Distribution networks deliver electricity from the wider system to homes, businesses, farms and industrial consumers.

The electricity grid connects these activities. It allows power from different generating stations to meet demand across connected areas. Electricity may also move between states through the wider interconnected network, so the location of a generating station and the location of a consumer need not be the same.

Key electricity institutions in Gujarat

Gujarat's electricity sector includes state-owned companies, private entities and regulatory institutions. Their functions are distinct.

InstitutionFull name or categoryMain function
GUVNLGujarat Urja Vikas Nigam LimitedHolding company; bulk power purchase and coordination of subsidiaries
GSECLGujarat State Electricity Corporation LimitedState-owned electricity generation
GETCOGujarat Energy Transmission Corporation LimitedState electricity transmission network
UGVCLUttar Gujarat Vij Company LimitedDistribution in its authorised northern Gujarat areas
DGVCLDakshin Gujarat Vij Company LimitedDistribution in its authorised southern Gujarat areas
MGVCLMadhya Gujarat Vij Company LimitedDistribution in its authorised central Gujarat areas
PGVCLPaschim Gujarat Vij Company LimitedDistribution in its authorised western Gujarat areas
GERCGujarat Electricity Regulatory CommissionElectricity regulation, including relevant tariffs, licences and standards
SLDCState Load Dispatch CentreState-level electricity-system operation and dispatch coordination

GUVNL is the holding company for GSECL, GETCO and the 4 state-owned distribution companies. These companies emerged from restructuring of Gujarat's former vertically integrated state electricity arrangements.

Torrent Power also operates as a licensed electricity distribution entity in specified areas of Gujarat. Consequently, the 4 Vij companies are the 4 state-owned regional distribution companies, not the only entities authorised to distribute electricity anywhere in the state.

The distinction between a transmission company and a distribution company

GETCO operates electricity transmission infrastructure. The regional Vij companies distribute electricity to consumers in their respective authorised service areas. The fact that a transmission line physically passes through a village does not make the transmission company the retail electricity supplier to that village.

Likewise, GERC regulates the electricity sector. It is not a power station, transmission company or ordinary electricity retailer. SLDC coordinates system operation so that generation and electricity demand can be balanced through the connected grid. Its role differs from determining retail tariffs.

Electricity losses and supply reliability

Not all electricity produced at a generating station becomes electricity billed to an end-user. Some energy is used within the generating station, and some is lost in the networks that transport and distribute electricity.

Technical losses arise from the physical operation of electrical equipment and networks. Commercial losses relate to problems such as incorrect metering, unauthorised use, inadequate billing and failure to collect payment.

Electricity reports use related but distinct indicators:

  • Transmission and distribution (T&D) losses: An indicator concerned with electricity lost across transmission and distribution systems under the reporting method used.
  • Aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses: A broader distribution-performance indicator that incorporates the effects of energy accounting, billing and collection efficiency.

AT&C losses should not automatically be treated as identical to T&D losses. Their definitions, calculation methods and reporting periods should be checked before comparing percentages.

Improved metering, maintenance, network operation and bill collection can reduce avoidable losses. Reliable electricity supply also depends on sufficient generation, adequate transmission and distribution capacity, and the ability to manage changing demand.

How the institutions support renewable energy

Renewable generating plants must be connected to suitable electricity networks before their power can serve consumers. New solar and wind capacity may therefore require transmission expansion, suitable operating arrangements and cooperation between generating companies, transmission operators, distribution companies and system dispatch authorities.

Increasing installed renewable capacity is only one part of the electricity transition. Delivering the generated electricity to the place and time of demand is equally important.

Prelims focus

  • GSECL is associated with electricity generation; GETCO with electricity transmission.
  • UGVCL, DGVCL, MGVCL and PGVCL are Gujarat's 4 state-owned regional distribution companies.
  • GUVNL is their holding and coordinating company along with GSECL and GETCO.
  • GERC is the state electricity regulator.
  • SLDC is associated with electricity-system operation and dispatch coordination.
  • Trap: Transmission, distribution and regulation are not the same activity.

[References: Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission, Annual Report 2022–23, section 5, 'The Power Sector Scenario in Gujarat'; Gujarat Power Research and Development Cell, Government of Gujarat initiative, 'About Us,' institutional roles, consulted 16 November 2026; Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Gujarat State Energy Efficiency Action Plan, institutional framework of the power sector; NCERT, Class 11 Economics, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 8, 'Infrastructure,' printed pp. 146–149.]
